Hi. I recently read @Leonardo de Moura 's article explaining how Lean avoids some correctness issues of other provers by having a small kernel checker that also has other implementations. That is good for soundness of proofs. What I'm wondering is whether there has been effort to prove the correctness of the compiler. If someone writes a program in Lean, it will have well defined semantics because Lean does (except, perhaps one would need to come up with definitions of the semantics of the outside world for IO). But can we prove that C code produced by the Lean compiler will correctly implement the program? That would require a formal C semantics, perhaps similar to the the input IR of CompCert and semantics of the runtime system. Do we need something like CompCert, only written in Lean?

I don't remember seeing anything written about Lean compiler correctness and thought this would be an interesting topic to discuss.

This is very hard. One note is that the Lean compiler is compiled using itself, so technically a proof in Lean that the Lean compiler is correct is insufficient. However, it's probably good enough for most practical purposes. This proof would itself be very hard to construct because the compiler uses things like the IO monad and partial functions.

As an alternative to proving that the Lean compiler is correct, you can instead have the Lean compiler be proof producing. This is the approach taken by Metamath C.

Also, the Lean compiler is itself a Lean metaprogram. And right now you can not reason about Lean metaprograms at all, most metaprogramming functions are partial or opaque. So even if you did want to put the effort into verifying the compiler, you can't even start. I'd love for this to change though.

Niels Voss said:

This is very hard. One note is that the Lean compiler is compiled using itself, so technically a proof in Lean that the Lean compiler is correct is insufficient. However, it's probably good enough for most practical purposes. This proof would itself be very hard to construct because the compiler uses things like the IO monad and partial functions.

leaving out the practical issues like partial functions and IO, why would this be insufficient? I don't see why this couldn't work in principle, just because it's used to compile itself doesn't mean you couldn't prove that it preserves the semantics (based on e.g. lean4lean). There's some issues with the runtime system too, you'd have to axiomatize and prove correct too (probably with some model of C's semantics), but I don't see why it matters that it happens to compile itself
Well, the problem is that if the compiler miscompiled itself, then you're proving correctness of the "correctly compiled" version and not the actual one that's running.

CakeML has a cool way of solving the bootstrapping problem that involves the compiler compiling itself and producing a correctness proof about the resulting compiler. The technique is described in a minimalist version in this paper:
https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~myreen/cpp2021-bootstrap-myreen.pdf
Reminds me of the 1984 classic "Reflections on Trusting Trust"

Robin Arnez said:

Well, the problem is that if the compiler miscompiled itself, then you're proving correctness of the "correctly compiled" version and not the actual one that's running.

the proof of the correctness would not be part of the compiler though, that's part of the type checker. The compiler wouldn't miscompile itself, otherwise the proof would not go through (or you'd have an incorrect assumption outside, in the part you've axiomatized)

To demonstrate the problem: lean4#13009 introduces a miscompilation into the compiler without touching any Lean code. This miscompilation also doesn't go away if you recompile Lean and perform a stage0 update (the miscompilation in question is that #eval 12321 produces 42). Even if you managed to prove the Lean code correct, the compiler still misbehaves. Of course, you could say that this example is very elaborate; but it shows that a proof of correctness on the level of the Lean code doesn't give you a 100% foolproof guarantee that the compiler actually behaves correctly.

@Robin Arnez how did you construct that example? It's a huge diff and very opaque, so it's hard to see tho point. Of course I agree that if you produce a broken runtime system then the behaviour will be broken. That's why I said that you'd need to verify the runtime too. I can't tell however, if there is genuinely some conceptual reason why stage0 could affect the correctness proof if you have a verified compiler (including the runtime system), maybe there is, but I don´t quite understand why
The last commit is not very helpful to look at but you can look at the two commits before that
It's was a similar process to producing a quine
hhm, but why would this not break the (hypothetical) proof?

It depends on which level you're writing the proof; if you're writing it on the level of the Lean code you won't find the modification I snuck into docs#Lean.Compiler.LCNF.ToLCNF.litToValue and you'd be able to just prove it correct (the term hasn't changed, after all). If you're doing it on the level of the C code, you'd obviously spot it eventually but I don't think that is realistic to do. One thing that could save you though is if you had another compiler you could trust (that isn't written in Lean) and use that to compile stage1.
In other words, proving the compiler correct means that if the compiler itself is not miscompiled, then it will behave correctly; but you can't be certain that you have that version of the compiler.
